stem: A developer adds `"use cache"` to an async data function in a Next.js 16 app and the build rejects it. What is missing?

options.text: `cacheComponents: true` in `next.config.ts`
options.why: `use cache`, `cacheLife` and `cacheTag` are Cache Components features and need this flag.

options.text: An `export const dynamic = "force-static"` in the page
options.why: That is a previous-model route segment option; it does not enable the directive.

options.text: A Redis cache handler configured under `cacheHandlers`
options.why: Without `cacheHandlers` Next.js falls back to an in-memory LRU cache; a handler is optional.

options.text: Wrapping the function in `unstable_cache` first
options.why: `unstable_cache` is the older API that `use cache` replaces, not a prerequisite for it.

explanation: In Next.js 16, `"use cache"` ships with Cache Components and is enabled by setting `cacheComponents: true` in the Next config. The same flag also turns on `cacheLife`, `cacheTag` and the `use cache: private` / `use cache: remote` variants. Without it, use the previous model: `fetch` options, `unstable_cache` and route segment config.

stem: In a Next.js 16 app that does not enable Cache Components, a plain `fetch(url)` in a Server Component is stored in the persistent server cache by default, as it was in Next.js 14.

options.text: True
options.why: Caching became opt-in in Next.js 15; a plain `fetch` with no `cache` option is not stored in the persistent cache.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: you opt in with `cache: "force-cache"` or `next.revalidate`. Without that, the request is only fetched once at build time if the route is prerendered.

explanation: The default is "auto no cache". The request is fetched on every request in development, and fetched once during `next build` only because the route is statically prerendered. If request-time APIs are used, it runs on every request. To store the response in the server cache, set `cache: "force-cache"` or a positive `next.revalidate`.

stem: A layout and a page both call `fetch("https://api.example.com/user")` with `GET` and identical options while rendering one request. Neither call sets `cache`. How many network requests leave the server for that render?

options.text: Two, because neither call opted into caching
options.why: Persistent caching is opt-in, but request memoization is separate and automatic.

options.text: One: identical `GET` fetches are memoized per render
options.why: Memoization deduplicates the calls across layouts, pages and components within one render.

options.text: Zero, because the response is served from the Data Cache
options.why: Nothing was stored persistently, so there is no cached response to serve.

options.text: One per component that renders the result on the client
options.why: Memoization happens on the server during rendering; client rendering does not trigger fetches.

explanation: `fetch` requests using `GET` with the same URL and options are automatically memoized during a server render pass, so Next.js executes the request once and shares the result. This is separate from persistent caching: memoization lasts only for one render pass, while cached responses persist across requests. You can opt out by passing an `AbortController` signal.

stem: Match each `cacheLife` property with what it controls.

options.text: How long the client router reuses the result without asking the server
After this age, the next request is served the cached result and triggers a background refresh
After this long with no traffic, the next request waits for fresh content
The `Cache-Control: max-age` value sent to the browser for the HTML

explanation: `stale` is client-side: the router shows cached content with no network request for that long, and the server sends it via `x-nextjs-stale-time` rather than `Cache-Control`. `revalidate` is server-side stale-while-revalidate: past it, the cached version is served and regenerated in the background. `expire` is the hard limit: after that long without requests, the next request regenerates synchronously.

stem: A `"use cache"` function never calls `cacheLife`, so the `default` profile applies. After how many minutes does the server revalidate its entry in the background? Type a number.
explanation: The `default` profile is stale 5 minutes, revalidate 15 minutes, expire never. The docs recommend pairing every cache directive with an explicit `cacheLife` so the lifetime is visible at the call site instead of depending on the default or on nested caches.

stem: Where can `updateTag("posts")` be called in a Next.js 16 app?

options.text: Only inside Server Actions
options.why: It is built for read-your-own-writes after a user mutation and throws anywhere else.

options.text: In Server Actions and Route Handlers
options.why: That is where `revalidateTag` works; `updateTag` in a Route Handler throws.

options.text: Anywhere on the server, including Proxy
options.why: Neither tag function runs in Proxy, and `updateTag` is narrower still.

options.text: In Client Components via an import from `next/cache`
options.why: Cache invalidation only works in server environments.

explanation: `updateTag` can only be called from Server Actions. It immediately expires the tagged data so the next request waits for fresh content, which is what you want right after the user changes something. From a Route Handler or webhook, use `revalidateTag(tag, profile)`, or `revalidateTag(tag, { expire: 0 })` for immediate expiry.

stem: A self-hosted ISR page returns the response header `x-nextjs-cache: STALE`. What happened?

options.text: The page was rendered fresh because nothing was cached yet
options.why: A cache miss with a fresh render is reported as `MISS`.

options.text: The cached page was served while it regenerates in the background
options.why: This is stale-while-revalidate in action: fast response now, fresh content shortly.

options.text: The page was regenerated by an on-demand revalidation call
options.why: On-demand regeneration is reported as `REVALIDATED`.

options.text: The cache entry expired, so the request blocked until fresh HTML was ready
options.why: A blocking regeneration does not serve the old page, so it is not reported as stale.

explanation: The `x-nextjs-cache` header shows how a cached route was served. `HIT` means served from cache, `STALE` means served from cache while revalidating in the background, `MISS` means not in cache and rendered fresh, and `REVALIDATED` means regenerated via on-demand revalidation. Combine it with `NEXT_PRIVATE_DEBUG_CACHE=1` to debug ISR behaviour.

options.text: Export `const tags = ["products"]` from the same module
options.why: There is no module-level tags export; tags are attached from inside a cache scope.

options.text: Call `cacheTag("products")` inside the function, after the directive
options.why: Tags are attached to the cache entry from inside its `use cache` scope.

options.text: Pass `{ tags: ["products"] }` as an argument to `getProducts`
options.why: Arguments only become part of the cache key; they do not tag the entry.

options.text: Nothing, because `updateTag` matches the function name
options.why: Tags are explicit strings; function names are never used as tags.

explanation: Use `cacheTag("products")` inside a `use cache` function or component, or `next: { tags: ["products"] }` on a `fetch` call. After that, `updateTag("products")` (Server Actions) or `revalidateTag("products", "max")` invalidates every entry with that tag. A single entry can carry several tags, for example `cacheTag("products", "catalog")`.

options.text: Only `filter`, because closures are invisible to the cache
options.why: Captured outer variables are bound as arguments, so they do enter the key.

options.text: The fetch URL, because the fetch inside decides the key
options.why: `use cache` keys on its own inputs, not on what the body fetches.

options.text: The build ID, the function ID, and both `userId` and `filter`
options.why: Captured variables become arguments, so each user and filter pair gets its own entry.

options.text: Nothing user-specific, so every user shares one entry
options.why: That would be a data leak; the captured `userId` prevents it.

explanation: A `use cache` key is built from the build ID (or `deploymentId`), a hash of the function's location and signature, its serializable arguments, and, in development, an HMR hash. Variables captured from enclosing scopes are automatically bound as arguments, so `userId` and `filter` are both in the key here.

stem:
This component fails at request time with the `next-request-in-use-cache` error. What is the recommended fix? ```tsx async function Greeting() { "use cache" const theme = (await cookies()).get("theme")?.value return

Theme: {theme}

} ```

options.text: Call `connection()` before reading cookies inside the cached scope
options.why: `connection()` is prohibited inside cache scopes as well.

options.text: Read the cookie in an uncached parent and pass `theme` as a prop
options.why: The value then becomes part of the cache key, and the cached scope stays request-free.

options.text: Wrap `Greeting` in `<Suspense>` so cookies can resolve later
options.why: Suspense handles streaming; it does not lift the ban on request APIs in cached scopes.

options.text: Switch to `"use cache: remote"`, which may read cookies directly
options.why: Remote caches also need runtime values passed in as arguments.

explanation: Cached functions cannot access `cookies()`, `headers()` or `searchParams`, and the restriction follows the call stack into helpers. The preferred pattern is to read the value outside the cached scope (behind `<Suspense>`) and pass it as an argument. `"use cache: private"` is the exception for functions that must read runtime data directly.

stem: Which values can be passed as arguments to a `"use cache"` function and still be used inside its body? (Choose three.)

options.text: A plain object such as `{ theme: "dark" }`
options.why: Plain objects are serializable with React Server Components rules.

options.text: A `Date`
options.why: Dates are in the list of supported argument types.

options.text: A `Map` of filter names to values
options.why: Maps, Sets, TypedArrays and ArrayBuffers are supported.

options.text: An instance of a `User` class
options.why: Class instances cannot be serialized for the cache key.

options.text: A `URL` object built from the request
options.why: `URL` instances are explicitly unsupported; pass the string instead.

options.text: A callback that the cached body calls
options.why: Functions are allowed only as pass-through values that the body never invokes.

explanation: Arguments use React Server Components serialization: primitives, plain objects, arrays, Dates, Maps, Sets, TypedArrays and ArrayBuffers. Class instances, functions, symbols, WeakMaps and URL instances are unsupported. Non-serializable values such as `children` or a Server Action can be accepted only as pass-through, as long as the cached body does not read or call them.

stem: A CMS webhook hits a Route Handler that calls `revalidateTag("posts", "max")`. Twenty pages use that tag. What happens next?

options.text: All twenty pages regenerate in the background straight away
options.why: Revalidation is triggered by requests, not by the `revalidateTag` call.

options.text: Each page is served stale on its next visit while it regenerates
options.why: Pages revalidate one by one as traffic arrives, with stale-while-revalidate.

options.text: The next visitor to each page waits for fresh content
options.why: That blocking behaviour comes from `updateTag` or `{ expire: 0 }`.

options.text: Nothing, because tags can only be revalidated from Server Actions
options.why: Route Handlers can call `revalidateTag`; only `updateTag` is limited to Server Actions.

explanation: `revalidateTag` marks tagged data as stale. The next request for that data starts a revalidation and is served stale content while it runs. The second argument sets how long stale content may be served; `"max"` is a one-year window. Because requests trigger the work, pages using the tag revalidate as they are visited rather than all at once.

stem: A page uses `"use cache"` with `cacheLife("hours")` and steady traffic. Put these events in the order they occur after the entry is first created.

options.text: Requests inside the first hour get the cached result
The first request after an hour gets the old result and starts a background regeneration
The regeneration finishes and the cache entry is replaced
Later requests get the freshly generated result

explanation: This is stale-while-revalidate. Until `revalidate` (1 hour for `hours`) the entry is fresh. The first request after that is still served immediately from cache, and it triggers regeneration in the background. Once the new version is stored, subsequent requests receive it. Only if the entry goes unrequested past `expire` (1 day for `hours`) does a request have to wait.

stem: `next.config.ts` rewrites `/blog` to `/news`, and the route file lives at `app/news/page.tsx`. A Server Action edits a post. Which call refreshes that page?

options.text: `revalidatePath("/blog")`, because users see that URL
options.why: The source path does not match the cache entry, so nothing is invalidated.

options.text: `revalidatePath("/news")`, the rewrite destination
options.why: Cache entries are tied to the route file that renders them.

options.text: `revalidatePath("/blog/page")`, adding the file name
options.why: Never append `/page`; use the optional `type` argument instead.

options.text: Both paths, because one alone never works with rewrites
options.why: Only the destination matches; the source call is wasted.

explanation: `revalidatePath` operates on the route file structure, not the URL in the address bar. With a rewrite from `/blog` to `/news`, pass the destination `/news`. Also remember that `revalidatePath` only refreshes that path: other pages using the same data keep their cache until their tags are revalidated.
reference: Next.js docs: revalidatePath (Using revalidatePath with rewrites)

stem: `/blog` and `/dashboard` both fetch posts with `next: { tags: ["posts"] }`. Calling `revalidatePath("/blog")` also gives `/dashboard` fresh posts on its next visit.

options.text: True
options.why: `revalidatePath` refreshes only the given path; `/dashboard` keeps its cached data.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: only `/blog` re-renders. `/dashboard` stays stale until the `posts` tag is revalidated.

explanation: `revalidatePath` invalidates a page or layout path, while `revalidateTag` and `updateTag` act on every page that uses a tag. The docs show exactly this case: after `revalidatePath("/blog")`, `/dashboard` still shows stale data. Pair `revalidatePath` with `updateTag("posts")` when both must stay consistent.

stem: An expensive report query should survive deployments so a release does not cause a burst of database load. The team uses `"use cache: remote"` with a Redis handler, but every deploy starts cold. Why?

options.text: Redis handlers flush themselves when the Next.js process restarts
options.why: The handler storage persists; the old entries simply stop being looked up.

options.text: Remote caches are cleared whenever `revalidatePath("/")` runs at build
options.why: Builds do not call revalidation functions on their own.

options.text: The cache key includes the build ID, so a new deploy uses new keys
options.why: This is intentional; use `unstable_cache` or the `fetch` cache to persist across deploys.

options.text: Remote entries are capped by `cacheMaxMemorySize`, which resets
options.why: That setting sizes the default in-memory cache, not a remote handler.

explanation: Every `use cache` key, including remote ones, contains the build ID or the configured `deploymentId`. A new build produces new keys and old entries are unreachable, which protects against serving values whose shape changed between releases. For data that must persist across deploys, the docs point to `unstable_cache` (non-`fetch`) or the `fetch` cache.
reference: Next.js docs: use cache: remote (Persistence across deploys)

stem: A Server Component calls `fetch(url, { cache: "force-cache" })`. Which statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Requests that differ only in headers get separate cache entries
options.why: A request matches on its URL, method, headers and body.

options.text: Only responses with a `200` status are stored
options.why: Error responses are fetched again next time rather than cached.

options.text: `POST` requests are never cached, even with this option
options.why: With `force-cache` any request can be cached, including `POST`.

options.text: Requests that send an `authorization` header are skipped
options.why: The docs say they are cached too, so be deliberate about it.

options.text: The entry is dropped on every deploy like a `use cache` entry
options.why: The `fetch` cache is the documented way to persist across deploys.

explanation: `force-cache` looks for a matching request in the server-side cache, matching on URL, method, headers and body. A fresh match is returned, a missing or stale one is fetched again, and only `200` responses are stored. Caching is opt-in and applies even to `POST` and authorized requests, so think about data sensitivity. Draft Mode bypasses the cache entirely.

stem: A `GET` Route Handler calls the same `fetch("https://api.example.com/rates")` twice, with no `cache` option. How many requests reach the upstream API?

options.text: One, because identical `GET` fetches are always memoized
options.why: Memoization is tied to the React render pass, and a Route Handler has none.

options.text: Two: memoization does not apply in Route Handlers
options.why: Route Handlers are not part of the React component tree.

options.text: Zero after the first deploy, served from the Data Cache
options.why: Nothing opted into the persistent cache here.

options.text: One, but only in production builds
options.why: Memoization never applies in Route Handlers, in any environment.

explanation: Automatic `fetch` memoization deduplicates calls during a server render pass across layouts, pages and components. Route Handlers are not part of the component tree, so memoization does not apply there. Fetch once and reuse the value, or cache the work with `use cache` or `force-cache`.

stem: A component sets `cacheLife({ stale: 5, revalidate: 900, expire: 86400 })`. The client router still reuses the result for a minimum number of seconds regardless of that value. What is that minimum? Type a number.
explanation: The client router enforces a minimum stale time of 30 seconds so prefetched links stay usable before the user clicks. It applies only to time-based expiry: calling `revalidateTag`, `revalidatePath`, `updateTag` or `refresh` from a Server Action clears the whole client cache immediately. A `stale` under 30 seconds also keeps the entry out of prerenders.

options.text: The `tags` option makes every tagged entry share one key
options.why: Next.js never uses tags to identify an entry; they only drive invalidation.

options.text: `userId` is a closure missing from both the arguments and key parts
options.why: Every user maps to the same `["orders"]` entry, so the first user's orders are served to all.

options.text: `unstable_cache` must be defined at module scope to key per user
options.why: Moving it would not help; the key still has to include `userId`.

options.text: Database calls are always shared across users unless a `fetch` is used
options.why: Non-`fetch` work can be keyed per user once the user ID is part of the key.

explanation: `unstable_cache` keys on its key parts, the arguments, and the stringified function. A closure variable is not covered, which is why the docs insist on adding closures to `keyParts` when they are not passed as parameters. Pass `userId` as an argument (`unstable_cache(async (id) => ..., ["orders"])` then `getOrders(userId)`) or add it to the key parts.

stem: A recommendations function reads `cookies()` deep inside a vendor helper, so it can't be refactored to take the value as an argument. The team marks it `"use cache: private"` with `cacheLife({ stale: 300 })`. Where can its result be reused?

options.text: In the server cache, shared by every user who sends the same cookie
options.why: Private caches are never stored on the server across requests.

options.text: In a remote cache handler configured under `cacheHandlers`
options.why: Custom handlers cannot be configured for `use cache: private`.

options.text: Within one request, and in that browser for the stale time
options.why: The browser keeps the output for the `stale` window; it never persists on the server.

options.text: Nowhere, because private caches only validate the directive
options.why: They do deduplicate within a request and cache on the client.

explanation: `"use cache: private"` allows `cookies()`, `headers()` and `searchParams` inside a cached scope. Matching calls within one request can share a result, and the client router may keep the rendered output for the `stale` time. Next.js does not store it in any server cache across requests, it can't use custom handlers, and it is excluded from the static shell.

stem: Which of these cache arrangements does Next.js 16 allow? (Choose two.)

options.text: A `"use cache: remote"` function called inside another remote cache
options.why: Remote caches can be nested inside other remote caches.

options.text: A `"use cache: remote"` function called inside a plain `"use cache"` function
options.why: Remote caches can be nested inside regular caches.

options.text: A `"use cache: remote"` function called inside a private cache
options.why: Remote caches cannot be nested inside private caches.

options.text: A `"use cache: private"` function called inside a remote cache
options.why: Private caches cannot be nested inside remote caches.

options.text: Calling `cacheLife("hours")` at module scope to set every export's lifetime
options.why: `cacheLife` must run inside a cache scope; at module scope it throws.

explanation: The nesting rules keep per-user data from leaking into shared storage. A remote cache may sit inside a remote or regular cache. Private and remote scopes cannot be nested inside each other in either direction. `cacheLife` and `cacheTag` only work inside a cache directive scope.
reference: Next.js docs: use cache: remote (Nesting rules)

stem: `Dashboard` uses `"use cache"` but never calls `cacheLife`. It renders `Stats` (`cacheLife("hours")`) and `Alerts` (`cacheLife({ revalidate: 300 })`). What server `revalidate` does `Dashboard`'s own entry end up with?

options.text: 15 minutes, because inner lifetimes never affect an outer cache
options.why: Without an explicit outer `cacheLife`, shorter inner lifetimes do propagate.

options.text: 1 hour, because the longest inner lifetime wins
options.why: Inner caches can shorten the default but never extend it.

options.text: 5 minutes, because the shorter inner lifetime wins
options.why: `Alerts` at 300 seconds pulls the implicit 15-minute default down.

options.text: It fails the build because inner lifetimes differ
options.why: Only a short-lived inner cache under an implicit outer lifetime is an error.

explanation: With no explicit `cacheLife`, the outer cache uses `default` (15 minute revalidate). Inner caches with shorter lifetimes reduce it, and longer ones cannot extend it. So `Stats` (1 hour) has no effect and `Alerts` (5 minutes) lowers it to 5 minutes. An explicit outer `cacheLife` would take precedence, which is why the docs recommend always setting one.

stem: A page marked `"use cache"` with no `cacheLife` renders a third-party `<LiveTicker />` that uses `cacheLife("seconds")` internally. What happens during `next build`?

options.text: The page silently becomes short-lived and leaves the static shell
options.why: Next.js refuses to let this happen silently.

options.text: Prerendering fails until the page sets an explicit `cacheLife`
options.why: This stops a hidden dependency from quietly shortening the page's lifetime.

options.text: The ticker is cached for 15 minutes because the outer default wins
options.why: An implicit outer lifetime can be shortened, not override the inner one.

options.text: The ticker is stripped from the page because it can't be cached
options.why: Nothing is removed; the build reports the misconfiguration.

explanation: A short-lived cache (the `seconds` profile, `revalidate: 0`, or `expire` under 5 minutes) would propagate into an outer cache that has no explicit lifetime. Because the nested cache may live in an imported module or a dependency, Next.js throws during prerendering instead. Fix it by setting `cacheLife` on the outer scope: a long one to stay static, or an explicitly short one behind `<Suspense>`.

stem: Four cached components use the preset profiles `default`, `minutes`, `hours` and `seconds`. Which one is left out of the prerendered static shell and resolved at request time?

options.text: `minutes`, because its 1-minute revalidate is too frequent
options.why: Revalidate only disqualifies at exactly 0; `minutes` expires after an hour.

options.text: `default`, because its expire is never
options.why: An unlimited expire is the most cacheable case, not the least.

options.text: `hours`, because its stale time is only 5 minutes
options.why: A 5-minute stale is the threshold for inclusion, not exclusion.

options.text: `seconds`, because its expire is only 1 minute
options.why: An expire under 5 minutes makes the cache a dynamic hole.

explanation: Prerendering excludes caches with `revalidate` of 0, `expire` under 5 minutes, or `stale` under 30 seconds. A `stale` of at least 30 seconds but under 5 minutes keeps it in prerenders but out of the App Shell. Of the presets, only `seconds` (stale 30 s, revalidate 1 s, expire 1 min) crosses a threshold, so it becomes a dynamic hole that should sit behind `<Suspense>`.

stem: A payment provider calls a webhook Route Handler when an invoice is voided. The invoice page must stop showing the old status at once, with no stale window. Which call should the handler make?

options.text: `updateTag("invoice-42")`, which expires the tag immediately
options.why: `updateTag` throws outside Server Actions, and a webhook is a Route Handler.

options.text: `revalidateTag("invoice-42", "max")`, the recommended profile
options.why: `max` serves stale content for up to a year while revalidating.

options.text: `revalidateTag("invoice-42", { expire: 0 })`
options.why: Stale content is never served, so the next request is a blocking miss.

options.text: `refresh()`, which forces the client router to refetch
options.why: `refresh` only works in Server Actions and refreshes the caller's router, not other users'.

explanation: Outside Server Actions you can't use `updateTag`. `revalidateTag` takes a second argument that sets how long stale content may be served. Passing `{ expire: 0 }` means it is never served, so the next request waits for fresh data. The deprecated single-argument form behaves the same way, but the docs ask you to pass the argument explicitly.

stem: Three Next.js pods sit behind a load balancer, each with the default cache. After a Server Action calls `revalidateTag("prices", "max")`, some users still see old prices indefinitely, depending on which pod serves them. What is the underlying fix?

options.text: Call `revalidateTag` three times so every pod receives it
options.why: The load balancer decides which pod gets each call, so repeats don't guarantee coverage.

options.text: Set `cacheMaxMemorySize` to a much larger value on every pod in the cluster
options.why: A bigger local cache keeps stale entries around longer, not shorter.

options.text: A shared handler that syncs tags via `updateTags` and `refreshTags`
options.why: Invalidations are local by default; shared tag state lets every pod learn about them.

options.text: Switch the action to `revalidatePath("/")`, which is global
options.why: Path revalidation uses the same per-instance tag system.

explanation: Revalidation events are local: calling `revalidateTag` on one instance only invalidates that instance's cache. A custom cache handler should write invalidations to shared storage in `updateTags()` and read them in `refreshTags()`, which runs before each request. Shared storage for entries reduces mismatches further. `refreshTags` must catch its own errors, or requests fail.
reference: Next.js docs: How revalidation works (Multi-instance considerations)

stem: Match each caching tool with how it behaves.

options.text: Shared across users, stored in memory per instance by default
Shared across users and instances in a durable handler, at the cost of a network lookup
Can read `cookies()` directly; results live only in the browser and the current request
Deduplicates calls within one render pass and is never reused across requests

explanation: Plain `use cache` stores entries in an in-memory LRU per instance unless a handler is configured, and serverless instances rarely reuse them. `use cache: remote` sends entries to a shared, durable handler for a higher hit rate, which costs storage and latency. `use cache: private` is per-client and can read request APIs. React `cache` only memoizes for the current render pass, and it is isolated inside `use cache` scopes.
reference: Next.js docs: use cache: remote (How it differs)

stem: Which inputs are part of a `"use cache"` entry's key in a production build? (Choose three.)

options.text: The build ID, or the `deploymentId` when configured
options.why: This is why entries never carry over to a new deploy.

options.text: A hash of the function's location and signature
options.why: The function ID separates different cached functions.

options.text: The serialized arguments, including captured closure variables
options.why: Different inputs produce separate entries.

options.text: The incoming request URL
options.why: Request data is not available in a cached scope, so it can't be keyed implicitly.

options.text: The user's cookies at the time of the call
options.why: Cookies must be read outside and passed in to affect the key.

options.text: An HMR refresh hash
options.why: That part of the key exists only in development.

explanation: The key combines the build ID (overridden by `deploymentId`), a secure hash of the function's location and signature, and the serialized arguments, with captured variables bound as arguments. In development an HMR refresh hash is added so edits invalidate entries. Request data never enters the key implicitly, which is why you must pass runtime values as arguments.

options.text: `from parent`, because React `cache` is shared per request
options.why: Inside `use cache`, React `cache` gets its own isolated scope.

options.text: `empty`, because `use cache` has an isolated React `cache` scope
options.why: Values stored outside the boundary are invisible inside it.

options.text: It throws, because React `cache` can't be called in a cached scope
options.why: It can be called; it just starts from a fresh scope.

options.text: `from parent` on the first request and `empty` afterwards
options.why: The scope is isolated on every call, not just after the first.

explanation: `React.cache` operates in an isolated scope inside `use cache` boundaries, so you can't use it to smuggle data into a cached function. This keeps cached output self-contained and predictable. Pass the data in as an argument instead, so that it also becomes part of the key.

stem: A cached function calls `cacheLife({ revalidate: 600 })` and nothing else. Omitted properties inherit from the `default` profile. What is its effective `expire`? Type one word.
explanation: Omitted properties in inline or custom profiles inherit from `default` (stale 5 minutes, revalidate 15 minutes, expire never). So this entry revalidates every 10 minutes in the background, keeps the 5-minute client stale time, and never hard-expires by time. If you set both `revalidate` and `expire`, `expire` must be longer than `revalidate`.

stem: When Draft Mode is enabled, every `"use cache"` function and component re-executes on each request, and the results are not written to the cache.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: drafts are always fresh without changing caching code. `draftMode().isEnabled` can be read inside the scope.

options.text: False
options.why: Draft Mode does bypass the cache; the docs describe it as always-fresh for cached functions.

explanation: With Draft Mode on, cached functions run every time and nothing is saved, so editors see unpublished content immediately. You may read `isEnabled` from `draftMode()` inside a `use cache` scope, but other request APIs are still forbidden. Calling `enable()` or `disable()` inside a cache scope throws.

stem: `next build` hangs for about 50 seconds and then fails with "Filling a cache during prerender timed out". Which code causes this?

options.text: Calling `cookies()` directly as the first line of a cached component
options.why: A direct call fails immediately with a different error, not a timeout.

options.text: Passing the un-awaited `cookies()` promise to a cached component
options.why: The cached function waits during the build for runtime data that never resolves.

options.text: Using `cacheLife("max")` on a component with many children
options.why: Long lifetimes do not slow down prerendering.

options.text: Calling `cacheTag` with more than 128 tags
options.why: Extra tags are dropped with a console warning; nothing hangs.

explanation: The timeout means a cached function is awaiting a promise that resolves to runtime or uncached data, created outside the cache boundary. Typical sources are promises passed as props, captured by closure, or pulled from a shared `Map`. Await the cookie store in the uncached parent and pass the plain cookie value to the cached component instead.

stem: The app has `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` and `app/blog/[slug]/[author]/page.tsx`. An action calls `revalidatePath("/blog/[slug]", "page")`. Which URLs are refreshed on their next visit?

options.text: Only the literal URL `/blog/[slug]`
options.why: A pattern with `type` matches every slug, not a path with brackets.

options.text: Every `/blog/<slug>` page, but not the `[author]` pages
options.why: The `page` type targets matching page files only, not deeper ones.

options.text: Every `/blog/<slug>` page and every `/blog/<slug>/<author>` page
options.why: That wider sweep needs `"layout"` as the type.

options.text: Nothing, because dynamic segments require a literal path
options.why: Patterns are supported, and `type` is then required.

explanation: With a dynamic segment, `revalidatePath` needs a `type`. `"page"` invalidates every path matching that page file but not pages beneath it, so `/blog/[slug]/[author]` is untouched. `"layout"` invalidates the layout at that segment, all nested layouts and all pages beneath. `revalidatePath("/", "layout")` purges everything.

options.text: Nothing: the last `cacheLife` call wins, so missing posts get `minutes`
options.why: The docs require only one `cacheLife` call per invocation; don't rely on ordering.

options.text: `cacheLife` must be the first statement and cannot appear in a branch
options.why: Calling it in branches is supported, as long as only one runs.

options.text: Returning `null` from a cached function is not serializable
options.why: `null` is a supported return value.

options.text: The missing-post path runs two `cacheLife` calls in one invocation
options.why: Move `cacheLife("days")` after the null check so each path makes exactly one call.

explanation: Conditional lifetimes are a documented pattern: `cacheLife("minutes")` in the not-found branch and `cacheLife("days")` for published content. The rule is that only one `cacheLife` call executes per invocation. Here the missing-post path runs both. Put the long lifetime after the early return, and add `cacheTag(`post-${slug}`)` so editors can invalidate a specific post.

stem: On a serverless deployment, `<CachedContent sessionId={...}>` uses `"use cache"` and is rendered behind `<Suspense>` after reading a cookie. Logs show its expensive body runs on almost every request. Which two statements explain it or fix it? (Choose two.)

options.text: Runtime entries live in per-instance memory that serverless instances rarely reuse
options.why: Gated content is not in the static shell, so it relies on that short-lived memory.

options.text: Moving it to `"use cache: remote"` with a shared handler raises the hit rate
options.why: A durable store shared by every instance keeps entries between requests.

options.text: Adding `cacheLife("max")` makes the in-memory entry persist across instances
options.why: A longer lifetime can't share memory between separate instances.

options.text: Switching to `"use cache: private"` stores the result on the server per session
options.why: Private caches never store results on the server across requests.

options.text: Raising `cacheMaxMemorySize` keeps entries alive between serverless invocations
options.why: More memory per instance doesn't help when each instance is short-lived.

explanation: Because `CachedContent` depends on request data, it isn't in the prerendered shell. At runtime the default handler is an in-memory LRU, and serverless instances are ephemeral, so entries are rarely reused. `use cache: remote` with a configured handler gives a cache shared across instances. It pays off at high hit rates, so key it on low-cardinality values.
reference: Next.js docs: Caching (Passing runtime values to cached functions)

stem: A product listing caches `getProducts(category, minPrice, maxPrice)` with `"use cache: remote"`. The Redis handler shows a hit rate near zero because shoppers use many price ranges. Which change best improves it?

options.text: Add `cacheLife("max")` so each price-range entry lives longer
options.why: Most price combinations are never requested twice, however long they live.

options.text: Switch to `"use cache: private"` so each shopper gets an entry
options.why: That moves caching to the browser and removes the shared server cache.

options.text: Cache by `category` only and filter prices in memory
options.why: Category has few unique values, so entries are reused across shoppers.

options.text: Add `cacheTag(category)` so entries are grouped under one key
options.why: Tags drive invalidation; they don't merge separate cache keys.

explanation: Every unique argument combination creates its own entry. The docs' guidance for remote caching is to find the dimension with fewer unique values (category rather than price, language rather than user ID), cache on it, and filter or select the rest in memory. Each entry holds more data, but cache misses against the backend cost more than the extra storage.
reference: Next.js docs: use cache: remote (Cache key considerations)

stem: A price widget uses `"use cache"` with `cacheLife({ stale: 10, revalidate: 60, expire: 3600 })`. Which statement about it is true?

options.text: Excluded from prerenders: a prefetch would go stale before a click
options.why: A `stale` under 30 seconds keeps the entry out of the static shell.

options.text: The client router reuses it for exactly 10 seconds before refetching
options.why: The router enforces a 30-second minimum for time-based staleness.

options.text: It is prerendered into the App Shell because `expire` is an hour
options.why: `expire` passes, but the short `stale` disqualifies it on its own.

options.text: The build fails because `stale` must be at least `revalidate`
options.why: No such rule exists; only `expire` must exceed `revalidate`.

explanation: Prerendering excludes caches with `stale` under 30 seconds, because prefetched content would expire before a user could click the link. `stale` between 30 seconds and 5 minutes keeps it in prerenders but out of the App Shell. Separately, the client router never treats time-based staleness as shorter than 30 seconds. The only cross-field check is that `expire` must be longer than `revalidate`.

stem: A Server Action ends with `revalidatePath("/", "layout")`. Which two statements describe the effect? (Choose two.)

options.text: The client cache is purged, so earlier routes refetch on navigation
options.why: Revalidation from a Server Action clears the client cache regardless of stale time.

options.text: All cached data is marked for revalidation on each route's next visit
options.why: The root layout covers every route beneath it.

options.text: Every page in the app is regenerated in the background straight away
options.why: Work happens when each path is next visited, not all at once.

options.text: Remote cache entries from earlier deploys are revived
options.why: Old builds' entries are unreachable because the build ID is in the key.

options.text: Only `app/page.tsx` is refreshed; other routes keep their cache
options.why: With `"layout"` the root layout and everything under it is invalidated.

explanation: `revalidatePath("/", "layout")` invalidates the root layout, all nested layouts and every page beneath them, so all cached data is revalidated on the next visit to each path. It also purges the client cache. It is the blunt instrument: prefer tag-based `updateTag` or `revalidateTag` to avoid over-invalidating.

stem: Two self-hosted instances share a custom cache handler backed by Redis. Put the steps in order, from a Server Action on instance A calling `revalidateTag("posts", "max")` to instance B serving fresh posts.

options.text: Instance A runs the action and calls `revalidateTag("posts", "max")`
The handler's `updateTags()` writes the invalidation timestamp to Redis
Before its next request, instance B's `refreshTags()` reads Redis and updates its local tag state
Instance B sees its entry predates the tag invalidation, serves it stale and regenerates
Later requests on instance B receive the regenerated posts

explanation: `updateTags()` runs when `revalidateTag` is invoked and should persist the event to shared storage. `refreshTags()` runs periodically, and always before a new request, to pull those events into local tag state. An entry whose timestamp is older than its tags' latest invalidation is stale. With the `max` profile it is served while regenerating, so fresh content arrives on later requests.
reference: Next.js docs: How revalidation works (Multi-instance considerations)

stem: An action calls `revalidateTag("catalog", "hours")`. The `hours` profile is stale 5 minutes, revalidate 1 hour, expire 1 day. What does passing `"hours"` control here?

options.text: The new entry's lifetime: it will now revalidate every hour
options.why: The regenerated entry keeps its own `cacheLife`; the profile here is about the stale window.

options.text: How long to wait before the revalidation is allowed to start
options.why: Revalidation starts on the next request, not after a delay.

options.text: The client stale time, so browsers keep the old data for 5 minutes
options.why: Server Action revalidation clears the client cache immediately.

options.text: Only its `expire`: stale for up to a day, then requests block
options.why: Within the window, requests get stale data while it revalidates.

explanation: The second argument to `revalidateTag` sets how long stale content may be served while revalidating. When you pass a profile name, only its `expire` is read, so `hours` gives a one-day window. Past it, a request waits for the revalidation to finish. `"max"` gives a one-year window and is recommended; `{ expire: 0 }` never serves stale content.

stem: Without Cache Components, match each `fetch` configuration in a Server Component with how Next.js 16 treats it.

options.text: Fetched once at build if reached before any request-time API, otherwise on every request
Fetched from the origin on every request, even with no request-time APIs on the route
Looked up in the server cache, matching on URL, method, headers and body
Never stored, preventing the resource from being cached

explanation: The default "auto no cache" rides on prerendering: a fetch reached before request-time APIs runs once at build, and later ones run per request. `no-store` always goes to the origin. `force-cache` uses the persistent server cache, keyed on the full request and storing only 200 responses. `revalidate: 0` prevents caching. Combining `revalidate: 3600` with `no-store` conflicts, and both options are ignored.

stem: In `next dev`, a Server Component uses `fetch(url, { cache: "no-store" })`. After editing an unrelated component and saving, the page still shows yesterday's data, but a full reload shows fresh data. Why?

options.text: `no-store` is ignored in development, so every fetch is cached
options.why: The source is hit on navigation and reload; only HMR refreshes reuse responses.

options.text: The client router cached the RSC payload for its 30-second stale time
options.why: This persists across edits regardless of time, so it isn't the router's stale window.

options.text: The Server Components HMR cache reuses fetches across hot reloads
options.why: This avoids repeated billed API calls; it is cleared on navigation or full reload.

options.text: The response was memoized and memoization survives between requests
options.why: Memoization lasts for a single render pass only.

explanation: In development Next.js caches `fetch` responses in Server Components across Hot Module Replacement, including the default and `no-store` options, for speed and to reduce billed API calls. Navigation or a full reload clears it. You can turn this off with `serverComponentsHmrCache: false`. Separately, a request with `cache-control: no-cache` (such as a hard refresh) bypasses fetch caching options in dev.

stem: Which statements about cache tags in Next.js 16 are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: Tags are case-sensitive, so `"Posts"` and `"posts"` are different tags
options.why: Both `revalidateTag` and `updateTag` document case-sensitive tags.

options.text: A tag longer than 256 characters is never assigned, so revalidating it does nothing
options.why: Over-long tags are skipped with a console warning.

options.text: After `revalidateTag`, each page revalidates when it is next requested
options.why: The call marks data stale; requests trigger the actual work.

options.text: Revalidating `"post"` also invalidates `"post-1"` and `"post-2"` by prefix
options.why: Tags are exact strings; there is no prefix or hierarchy matching.

options.text: Revalidating a tag immediately re-renders every page that uses it
options.why: Nothing renders until a request arrives for each page.

options.text: One `cacheTag` call can attach an unlimited number of tags
options.why: A single call accepts up to 128 tags; extras are dropped with a warning.

explanation: Tags are exact, case-sensitive strings of up to 256 characters, with up to 128 per `cacheTag` call. Applying the same tag twice has no extra effect. Invalidation is lazy: `revalidateTag` marks data stale and each page revalidates when requested. To invalidate related entries, tag them with a shared tag, for example `cacheTag("posts", `post-${id}`)`.

stem: You are writing a custom handler for `cacheHandlers`. An entry for `/blog/hello` was stored at timestamp 100. At 200, a Server Action calls `revalidatePath("/blog/hello")`. On the next request, `get()` receives soft tags such as `_N_T_/blog/layout` and `_N_T_/blog/hello`, and `getExpiration()` for them returns 200. What should `get()` do?

options.text: Return the entry as fresh, because no explicit `cacheTag` was revalidated
options.why: Path revalidation works through soft tags, which must be honoured.

options.text: Treat it as stale: a soft tag was invalidated after it was stored
options.why: An invalidation newer than the entry's timestamp makes it stale.

options.text: Throw an error so Next.js renders the route fresh
options.why: A thrown error propagates as a render error; return `undefined` for a miss.

options.text: Delete every entry whose path starts with `/blog`
options.why: Only entries carrying the invalidated soft tags are affected.

explanation: `revalidatePath` works through soft tags: auto-generated `_N_T_` tags for the leaf route and each ancestor layout. The handler compares the latest invalidation timestamp for those tags with the entry's own timestamp; if the invalidation is newer, the entry is stale. On internal errors, `get()` should return `undefined` (a cache miss) rather than throw, because the framework does not catch it.
reference: Next.js docs: How revalidation works (Soft tags)
